## 3. Rules and style decisions made in this conversation

These are not all in the standing docs yet. The why matters as much as the rule.

### Approval
1. **Approval is per date, and nothing is written to the live folder until all seven days of a cycle are approved.** Then all seven go in together. Bart stated this twice. I had written single approved days to the live folder and had to pull them back out.
2. **A "go" that arrives alongside a correction is not approval of the whole batch.** On 2026-09-19 Bart said "October 1 is good," later said "Go" while also giving a reminder about single verses, and I treated that as approval for all seven. It was not. Name the exact dates a go covers before writing anything.
3. **Drafts never sit in the live devotionals folder,** not even with `status: draft`. That field has never been verified as something the site honors. Held drafts go in `devotionals-2027/october-drafts/`.
4. **Bart does not have to be reminded how the system works.** He has shipped 300 of these. Do not explain the publish-date behavior or similar basics back to him.

### Scripture selection
5. **There is no four-verse limit and no license to skip verses.** Bart ruled this directly on 2026-09-29: "There is no rule that authorizes skipping of anything. Also no rule that says 4 verses is the max." The standing docs still describe a roughly four-verse norm and a skip technique (failure modes 25 and 28), both written up from earlier sessions rather than given by Bart. **Those notes should be corrected.** Because of this ruling, October 13 was restored to the full Luke 10:38-42 and nothing is trimmed for length any more. Passages set aside only for length are usable again, including Matthew 18:23-35, the unforgiving servant, which an earlier session dropped at thirteen verses.
6. **Single verses are allowed only when they are genuinely a complete thought.** Bart's reminder, 2026-09-19. John 3:27 failed this test, because it opens "John answered" in reply to a question that is not quoted and the sentence runs on into the next verse. It was expanded to John 3:27-30, which closes the quotation and names the Christ, and the post became "He Must Increase."
7. **Still enforced from the standing docs:** no duplicate passages, and no reuse of the same block of text (same chapter, same story, same paragraph) even with different verse numbers. Check the index end to end for every arc. Verify every replacement passage from scratch, since a swap is a brand new candidate.

### Writing
8. **Do not put words into a passage that are not in it.** Bart caught this on October 29, which used "illegal" and "theft" about Shebna's tomb. Isaiah 22 says neither. The actual charge in the text is about standing: "What have you to do here, and whom have you here." The post was rewritten to stay inside the text. The pattern to avoid is introducing a frame the text never raises in order to pre-empt a reader's objection.
9. **Do not tell a leader that ordinary, affectionate language is wrong.** The first October 2 draft treated "my people" as a warning sign. Bart, who is a founder, pushed back. Calling a team "my people" usually means responsibility and loyalty. The post now says that plainly and locates the problem in posture, where the word shifts from "mine to care for" into "mine to use."
10. **Founders break lazy framing.** The same October 2 draft argued that the ground under a leader was laid before they arrived. Bart founded his company and laid that ground himself. The rewrite names a founding underneath the founder's own: a founder builds a company, God made the world it sits in and the people who walk through its doors.
11. **No week-relative language inside a post.** No "this week," no "yesterday's passage," no "back in the first week," and no naming another post's date. Weeks shift from year to year and these posts will be rescheduled for 2027. Month-theme references are acceptable while months keep their order. "This week" inside a Practical Application bullet is fine, because that means the reader's own week.
12. **Run the voice check on every day before showing a batch to Bart,** not just before publishing. In September a devotional drafted in chat shipped with a banned phrase and blocked the site's deploys for about three hours. On 2026-09-19 the check caught "when it comes to" in October 2 after Bart had already posted it to Facebook; he changed it on Facebook himself and approved "where people are concerned."
13. **Every reflection must contain the literal theme word.** "Stewardship" appeared in all 31 October posts. October 14 initially said "stewards" and had to be fixed. November needs "thankful" or "thankfulness" in every reflection.
14. **Vary sentence construction across a batch.** Read all seven back to back before presenting. Three paragraphs in the October 8 to 14 batch were rewritten because they leaned on the same "a leader who does X, a leader who does Y" shape.
15. **Reflections run about 200 to 260 words,** five paragraphs, matching the May through July benchmark. Pull and read a real recent file before drafting rather than working from a remembered standard.

### Facebook
16. **Each post now gets a suggested first comment,** Bart's idea, because the Group has readers but no conversation. It is a short, positive, relevant question. It is kept separate from the post and is NOT written into the markdown file. If a `first_comment` field gets added for 2027, that is the place for it.
17. Group posting stays manual until the Page exists.

## 4. Facts, paths and sources a new session needs

- **Devotional markdown:** `ao-knowledge-hq-kit/journal/devotionals/`
- **Index, auto-generated:** `notes/DEVOTIONAL_INDEX.md` via `node scripts/generate-devotional-index.mjs`. Regenerate and read it fresh before any arc work. It held 301 entries after October 28.
- **Standing docs:** `~/Downloads/DEVOTIONAL_MASTER_CONTEXT.md`, `DEVOTIONAL_PROCESS_RULES.md`, `DEVOTIONAL_SESSION_LOG.md`, `DEVOTIONAL_HANDOFF.md`. These are outside the repo, so confirm they made it to the new Mac.
- **Real ESV text:** `https://archetypeoriginal.com/api/esv/passage?reference=Book+C:V-V` using curl with redirects followed. The local `.env.local` key is blank, so the local route cannot be used. More than about six calls at once returns a rate-limit error, so run them one at a time with a short pause. A bash read-loop with curl hangs; a small Python script works.
- **Voice check:** `detectVoiceViolationsInProse` from `lib/ao/voiceGuardrails.js`, plus `node scripts/verify-voice.mjs` for the whole corpus.
- **Publish steps:** copy the approved files into the devotionals folder, run `node scripts/generate-devotional-index.mjs`, run `node scripts/build-knowledge.mjs`, run `node scripts/verify-voice.mjs`, then stage the new posts along with `public/knowledge.json`, `data/knowledge-full.json` and `notes/DEVOTIONAL_INDEX.md`, commit and push. Pull first; the remote moves on its own because of the hourly routine.
- **Live site:** `https://archetypeoriginal.com/faith`. Check live status against the site or GitHub, never against local files.
- **ESV rights:** Bart already has Crossway API permission for the site. For the book, the plan is to send Crossway the finished manuscript for approval once it is written. Crossway allows up to 500 quoted verses without a license, and 365 printed passages will likely exceed that, so the approval matters.
- **Rework workspace:** `devotionals-2027/`, which is in `.gitignore` and therefore local only. It holds `posts/` with byte-identical copies of all 273 posts as of 2026-09-19, `REWORK_AUDIT.md`, and `october-drafts/`. **None of this reaches the new Mac.** The audit findings are summarized in section 5 so the work is not lost, but the folder itself has to be rebuilt by copying the live posts again.

## 5. The 2027 rework audit, summarized

Bart's instructions: work only on copies in a separate folder, never on the live posts. The audit ran on 2026-09-19 against all 273 posts.

**Approved by Bart 2026-10-27: "Yes, the audit is approved."** The audit's sorting is the rework plan: each post gets the treatment the audit assigned it (new passage, new reflection on the same passage, light edit, reschedule, or keep). The items the audit marks "Bart decides" are still his individual calls, and the Easter rescheduling below is still a recommendation. October through December 2026 were not in the audit and still need the same pass.

Headline findings:

- **38 posts need a different passage.** Nine in January, eleven in February.
- **63 need rewriting on the same passage,** mostly to reach the May through July depth.
- **44 need light edits. 2 need only rescheduling. 126 can stay as they are,** nearly all of May through September.
- **Average reflection length by month:** January 96 words, February 131, March 105, April 128, against 156 to 207 for May through July. January through March also close with "Today I will" instructions rather than an observation.
- **Six exact duplicate passages** exist, including James 4:6, Galatians 6:2, Colossians 3:23-24, 1 Corinthians 13:4-7, James 1:19-20 and Mark 10:42-45.
- **Hidden duplicates where one passage quotes another:** Hebrews 12:5-6 quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 and they ran on back-to-back days in September. Ephesians 4:25 quotes Zechariah 8:16, two days apart in July. 1 Peter 3:10 quotes Psalm 34:12-13, also two days apart in July. 2 Thessalonians 3:13 nearly repeats Galatians 6:9. Joshua 1:9 and Deuteronomy 31:6 are nearly the same charge.
- **Title collisions:** January 13 and January 24 share a title. January 6 and January 16 are near-rewrites of each other with the same closing line.
- **15 August and September posts** use week-relative wording that has to be rewritten.
- **Easter.** Bart wants the passion sequence to end on Easter Day with the resurrection. In 2026 Easter was April 5 but the resurrection post ran April 28. **Easter 2027 is March 28, Palm Sunday is March 21, and Easter 2028 is April 16.** My recommendation, not yet approved: move April's posts day for day into March, move the self-control material to March 31 through April 30, and schedule by distance from Easter (for example an `easter_offset` field) so later years need no hand rescheduling. Good Friday then lands on "It is finished," Saturday on the burial, Sunday on the resurrection. Feb 14, which is personal and about Carie, and July 4 should stay on fixed dates.
- **Other rework requirements from Bart:** monthly intros and summaries written separately from the last post of the month, for the book; `/faith` flushed and restarted with the reworked schedule; Auto's job limited to scheduling and publishing to `/faith` and the Facebook Page; and a running record of what gets written so a fresh set of 365 posts can be planned for 2028.

### YouVersion research, 2026-09-19
- Partner applications appear to be **paused for authors and creators in North America**. Unclear whether a small organization writing in English qualifies. Ask partnerships@youversion.com.
- **400 words maximum per day.** Our current posts exceed that, so YouVersion would need a shorter version linking back to the full one.
- Plans are **uploaded whole with a fixed launch date**, with no daily release, so there is nothing for Auto to automate there. Readers each start on their own day.
- Recommendation: package as **12 monthly plans** rather than one 365-day plan, since completion drops off badly past about three weeks.
- Passages are entered as references, so readers most likely see their own chosen Bible version rather than ESV. Not confirmed.
- The partner agreement is not public, so exclusivity and whether already-published content is allowed are both unknown. Get the agreement before committing.

### 2026-10-29-a-tomb-for-yourself.md
- title: "A Tomb for Yourself", slug: a-tomb-for-yourself
- scripture_reference: "Isaiah 22:15-16 (ESV)" with an en dash in the range
- summary: "A steward who starts carving a legacy into the rock has decided the position exists for them rather than for the household."

Reflection:

> The man in question has a title and a house to run. He is named as a steward, the one over the household, which means the resources, the staff and the authority all pass through his hands. What he has done with that is cut himself a tomb in the rock.
>
> The tomb is personal, permanent and impossible to miss. Cut out on the height, carved into the rock, built to outlast the man and to say something about him long after he is gone. The question that comes back to him is about standing. What have you to do here, and whom have you here.
>
> That question asks what claim he actually has on the place. A steward was handed a household to run, and he has treated the location as somewhere to establish himself permanently. Leaders do the same thing without ever touching a budget. A reputation built on the organization's platform. Relationships cultivated so they follow the person out the door. A legacy carved into the spot where the work was supposed to go.
>
> Stewardship assumes the position is temporary and the household is the point. A steward who starts carving a legacy into the rock has already decided, whether or not they would say it out loud, that the job exists for them.
>
> There is also the matter of who is asking. The question comes from someone with the standing to ask it, which is the part leaders tend to forget. Positions come with an owner, and owners eventually want to know what the position produced for the household rather than for the one holding it.

Practical Application: Name what you have built with your position that will leave with you rather than stay. / Ask what your title has produced for the people it was given to serve. / Separate the legacy you want from the work you were actually handed.

Takeaways: A steward can misuse a position without ever mishandling money, which is why this goes unexamined. / Positions come with an owner, and owners ask what the household gained.

Closing Thought: The tomb was impressive, and it was carved on someone else's time.

First comment for Facebook: What is something you built in a role that outlasted you there? Those are the ones that count.

### 2026-10-30-no-ground-for-complaint.md
- title: "No Ground for Complaint", slug: no-ground-for-complaint
- scripture_reference: "Daniel 6:3-4 (ESV)" with an en dash
- summary: "Stewardship done well is boring under inspection, with no side arrangement to explain and no number that needs context."

Reflection:

> Daniel is distinguished above the other officials and about to be set over the whole kingdom. That also makes him the most examined man in the administration, which is how it usually works when someone is about to be promoted past their peers.
>
> The search against him is hostile and specific. They are looking for a ground for complaint with regard to the kingdom, which means his actual work. The records, the decisions, the handling of what was entrusted to him. They find nothing, and the text gives the reason plainly. He was faithful.
>
> Most leaders are never audited by enemies. They get audited by circumstance. A bad quarter. A lawsuit. An unexpected departure. Someone finally looking closely at a process nobody had examined in years. Faithfulness over the long stretch is what determines whether that look turns up anything.
>
> Stewardship done well is boring under inspection. No side arrangement that needs explaining. No number that only makes sense with context. No favor that reads differently in writing than it sounded in the room.
>
> An excellent spirit was in him sits alongside the faithfulness rather than substituting for it. Daniel was both capable and clean, and that combination is what made him impossible to remove through ordinary means.

Practical Application: Pick the part of your work least likely to be examined and examine it yourself. / Find anything that would need explaining if someone read it cold, and fix the thing rather than the explanation. / Ask whether your competence has been covering for a practice you would not want examined.

Takeaways: Most leaders are audited by circumstance rather than by enemies, and the result depends on what was built beforehand. / Capability does not substitute for faithfulness, and leaders who have both are hard to dislodge.

Closing Thought: They went looking for something and the search came back empty.

First comment for Facebook: Have you ever been glad someone looked closely at your work? What had you done to be ready?

### 2026-10-31-for-such-a-time-as-this.md
- title: "For Such a Time as This", slug: for-such-a-time-as-this
- scripture_reference: "Esther 4:13-14 (ESV)" with an en dash
- summary: "The position arrived before the moment did, and keeping silent inside it is also a decision about what the position was for."
- This file carries `### October Overview` BEFORE the Scripture section, in the July 31 and August 31 format.

October Overview:

> October asked what a leader actually does with what has been entrusted to them. September spent a month on grace and mercy extended outward to people who had not earned it. Stewardship is the question that follows. If so much of what a leader holds was given rather than earned, the work is to tend it faithfully for as long as they are the one holding it.
>
> We started with where stewardship begins. A garden with two instructions attached, work it and keep it. The earth and everyone on it belonging to the LORD, which includes every person a leader oversees. An earth genuinely given to human hands, with real authority and real consequences. Strangers and sojourners holding land they could use but never sell in perpetuity. A warning against the sentence spoken in the heart, my power and the might of my hand. A platform that could not be received unless it was given. And an open hand that blessed the name of the LORD while grieving a loss.
>
> Then time, the one entrusted resource that cannot be earned back. A prayer to know the measure of our days. A plan held as a request rather than a guarantee. Autumn plowing that decides a harvest months before anyone goes looking for it. An ant with no officer over her. Work done with your might inside a window that closes. One necessary thing protected from a long list of good ones. And rest called for in the middle of the work rather than after the collapse.
>
> Then resources. Knowing the real condition of the flock rather than the reported condition. Wages earned and dropped into a bag with holes. An ox that brings the mess and the harvest in the same animal. Fragments gathered in a season of plenty, when nothing forced the care. Edges left standing in the field on purpose. Wealth that sprouts wings while a leader is looking right at it. And generosity that is ready before the moment arrives.
>
> Then people, which is where stewardship costs the most. Jacob absorbing twenty years of losses that were never his fault. Wages paid before the sun sets, because the worker is counting on it. Good not withheld when the power to give it is already in hand. The same share for the one who stayed with the baggage. Confidences kept when sharing them would have been useful. The rare person genuinely concerned for someone else's welfare. And a leader spent on people rather than spending them.
>
> We closed with position. A steward carving himself a tomb with access that came with the job. A man examined by enemies who found nothing, because he was faithful. And a queen told plainly that her position would not protect her and that the deliverance would come either way.
>
> November turns to thankfulness. Not gratitude as a mood that arrives when results are good, but thankfulness as a practice a leader keeps on purpose, including in the years when there is little to show. A leader who has spent a month accounting for what was entrusted to them is in a position to notice how much of it was given in the first place.
>
> The year will finish in Advent, preparing for what is to come. That is the work of every leader who has ever had to get a house, a team or a family ready for something they could see arriving and could not control.

Reflection:

> Mordecai's message does two things at once. It tells Esther that her position will not protect her, and it tells her that deliverance will come with or without her. Both are uncomfortable, and both are true of nearly every leadership position.
>
> Relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place. The work does not depend on her. That strips the flattery out of the request and leaves the real question, which is not whether she is essential but whether she will spend what she was given while she still has it.
>
> Who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this. The position arrived before the moment did. She did not plan for this and could not have, and now the thing she happens to hold is exactly what the moment requires.
>
> Stewardship turns out to be that specific. A leader is holding access, relationships, a budget, a platform or a seat at a particular table, and sooner or later something arrives that only that combination can address. Keeping silent is also a decision about what the position was for.
>
> Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape is the part leaders skip. Keeping your head down inside a position feels safer than spending it. Here it would not have been safer at all, and the month closes on that note rather than on a comfortable one.

Practical Application: Name the thing you are holding that the current moment actually requires. / Consider what keeping quiet would cost, including what it would cost you. / Spend some part of your position on something that will not benefit you.

Takeaways: The position arrives before the moment does, which is why faithfulness has to be built in advance. / Staying quiet inside a position is a decision about what the position was for.

Closing Thought: The palace was never the protection she thought it was.

First comment for Facebook: October was about what we do with what we were handed. What has this month made you look at differently?

## 9. Traps worth knowing

- **Do not regenerate content after a session reset without asking Bart first.** In September a full approved week was regenerated from scratch because a summary described it as unwritten. He had already posted it to Facebook. Ask whether he already has it.
- **The remote moves on its own.** An hourly routine commits and rebuilds. Always pull before committing, and expect to be several commits behind.
- **`devotionals-2027/` is ignored by git on purpose,** so a blanket "commit everything" will not sweep in 273 copies of published posts. Do not remove that line without a reason.
- **Local files are not evidence about the live site.** Check the site or GitHub.
- **A peer session cannot approve content.** Only Bart approves, in his own words.
